title: E-Commerce Order History Endpoint N+1 Query & Composite Index Optimization
businessContext: An e-commerce order history dashboard page (`/api/account/orders`) takes 14 seconds to load for loyal customers with 150 orders. Database CPU utilization reaches 98% during peak browsing hours.
problemStatement: The ORM repository performs 1 query to fetch the user's orders, and then inside a loop executes separate SQL queries to fetch line items, shipping addresses, and tracking status for each individual order (N+1 query problem). Additionally, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows a Sequential Scan on the 20-million row `orders` table because queries filter by `user_id` and sort by `created_at DESC` without a composite index.
constraints: Eliminate N+1 queries using `JOIN`, `DataLoader`, or batch `IN (...)` fetching.
Design composite index to enable Index Only Scan or fast B-Tree index scan.
Endpoint response time must drop under 80ms.
candidateTasks: Explain the N+1 query problem and how it impacts database connection pool latency.
Refactor queries into either a single JOIN query with JSON aggregation (`json_agg`) or a 2-query batch fetch using `WHERE order_id = ANY($1)`.
Provide the exact PostgreSQL DDL for the composite index: `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC)`.
hints: In PostgreSQL, `json_agg` or `jsonb_agg` lets you fetch orders with their nested line items in a single query.
A composite index `(user_id, created_at DESC)` satisfies both the WHERE filter and the ORDER BY sort without a temporary filesort.

testCases.name: Combines queries and uses composite index
testCases.explanation: Replaces 51 queries with a single indexed query.

alternativeApproaches: Two-query approach: Query 1 fetches 50 orders; Query 2 fetches items WHERE order_id = ANY(orderIds); stitch together in application memory.
Using GraphQL / DataLoader to batch and cache item lookups.
commonMistakes: Creating two separate single-column indexes on user_id and created_at instead of a single composite index.
Ordering index columns as (created_at, user_id), which does not help equality filtering on user_id.
